title: Decimal to Per Cent
context: Grade 5, the page on decimals as per cents. An adult may expect to multiply. What the page is doing is reading hundredths: a decimal is a number of hundredths, and the number of hundredths is the per cent. No chapter so far multiplies a decimal, so the route runs decimal, hundredths, per cent, and the % sign is kept every time.

writeup.why: Write a decimal as a per cent by reading it as hundredths, with the % sign kept, including tenths, decimals above one and whole numbers.
writeup.look: A decimal card over a row of hundred grids, one for each whole, the Hundredths counter, a fraction card and a per cent card, and the % sign tile.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Decimal to Per Cent' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the Hundredths counter, the hundredths shaded across every grid. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The decimal card stands at x 110, y 220, 300 by 110, its digits deep blue and its point in near-black ink, with a grey 0 labelled Place holder wherever a zero holds a place open. Up to four hundred grids, each 220 by 220, stand in a row from x 110, y 400, 30 apart, each labelled Whole and 100%. Cells fill deep blue, whole grids first. The Hundredths counter stands at x 450, y 230, with the % sign tile in its tray at x 450, y 310. The Read as hundredths and Split tenths buttons stand at x 690, y 230 and x 690, y 310. When a tenth is split, its column is cut into ten cells counted in amber. The fraction card and the per cent card stand at x 930, y 220 and x 930, y 310, and the per cent card turns green when it matches. Until the sign tile is placed, the per cent card shows that many whole grids, faded to half strength. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key and a % key, for typing a decimal, a whole number or a per cent. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The cards show the last decimal beside its hundredths and its per cent, with the grids filled under it.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, the instant the first grid fills, it gives a small bounce and the count rolls on into the second grid without stopping, the per cent card ticking past one hundred.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing filled yet. On the first phase the decimal card sits over one empty grid, with the % sign tile in its tray. On the second the card shows tenths over a grid with whole columns shaded. On the third it shows a decimal above one over two grids. On the fourth it holds a whole number over a row of empty grids. One thing moves, once: the Read as hundredths button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any decimal or whole number, read as hundredths, split into tenths and counted. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on hundredths, tenths, decimals above one and whole numbers as per cents.
voiceLines: A decimal, and hundred grids waiting to be filled.
Read it as hundredths. How many hundredths is it?
Each column is one tenth. Cut it into ten. How many hundredths now?
One whole grid is a hundred hundredths. Keep counting into the next.
Each whole is a hundred per cent. How many wholes are there?
A new decimal. How many hundredths is it?
Free play. Fill, split and count as many grids as you like.
Read it as hundredths again, one column at a time.
Every decimal became hundredths, and every answer kept its sign.

source_tool.description: A decimal card stands at the top of the working area, its digits deep blue and its point in near-black ink, with a grey 0 wherever a zero holds a place open. Under it stand up to four hundred grids in a row, each 220 by 220, labelled Whole and 100%. A Read as hundredths button fills the grids cell by cell in deep blue, whole grids first, while a Hundredths counter climbs. A Split tenths button cuts each shaded column of ten, one tenth, into its ten hundredths and counts them in amber. A fraction card writes the count over 100, and a per cent card writes the same count with the % sign, turning green when the child's answer matches. The % sign is a tile the child places; until it is placed, the per cent card shows that many whole grids, drawn faded to half strength. On the last phase the card holds a whole number and only whole grids fill. A number pad types a decimal, a whole number or a per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the Hundredths counter.
source_tool.art_direction: Hundred grids on squared paper / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read it as hundredths again, one column at a time.
voice.onNext: A new decimal. How many hundredths is it?
voice.opening: A decimal, and hundred grids waiting to be filled.
voice.onFinish: Every decimal became hundredths, and every answer kept its sign.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fill, split and count as many grids as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has read decimals aloud as hundredths and shaded them on squared paper. The tool is what fills the grids cell by cell and splits each tenth into ten, so the count of hundredths is seen rather than told.

answer_key.rule: Read the decimal as hundredths, and the number of hundredths is the per cent, with the % sign kept. Tenths become hundredths as ten times as many: each tenth is 10 hundredths. Each whole is 100 hundredths. So an amount above one whole is above 100%. A whole number is that many lots of 100%, and the same comes from (whole number x 100)% with the brackets written. The route is always decimal, then hundredths, then per cent. Without its % sign the answer would mean wholes.
answer_key.wrong: The grids are shown again with the child's count of hundredths shaded beside the decimal's own, each full grid labelled 100 hundredths, so the two counts are seen side by side, and the place the two part is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Per cent means out of a hundred, so 39 hundredths is 39%.
Keep the % sign on the answer.
items.question: Write 0.39 as a per cent.
items.checkpoint: The number of hundredths is the per cent.
items.misconception: Writing 0.39%, which puts the sign on the decimal and names less than one hundredth.

steps: Each tenth is 10 hundredths, so 9 tenths is 90 hundredths.
items.question: What per cent is 0.9?
items.checkpoint: Tenths become hundredths as ten times as many.
items.misconception: Writing 9%, which counts the tenths as if they were hundredths.

steps: 0.08 is 8 hundredths, with 0 holding the tenths place.
So 2.08 is 208 hundredths, and 2.08 = 208/100, which is 208%.
It is more than 100%, because 2.08 is more than one whole.
items.question: What per cent is 2.08?
items.checkpoint: Each whole is 100 hundredths. So an amount above one whole is above 100%.
items.misconception: Writing 280%, which skips the zero holding the tenths place.

items.question: What per cent is 7?
items.checkpoint: Each whole is 100%, so a whole number is that many lots of 100%.
items.misconception: Writing 7%, which is seven hundredths of one whole, not seven wholes.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: What per cent is 0.4?
items.final_answer: 40%, because 0.4 is 4 tenths, which is 40 hundredths

items.question: Write 0.2 and 0.02 as per cents.
items.final_answer: 0.2 is 20 hundredths, so 20%. 0.02 is 2 hundredths, so 2%

items.question: What per cent is 3.6?
items.final_answer: 360%, because 3 wholes are 300 hundredths and 6 tenths are 60 hundredths

teaching_notes: Read every decimal aloud as hundredths before the tool opens: nought point four seven is forty-seven hundredths. The number of hundredths is the per cent, and the % sign stays on it. Tenths become hundredths as ten times as many. The route is always decimal, then hundredths, then per cent, and the chapter teaches no other route for decimals. A whole number is that many lots of 100%. Use fresh decimals: the exercise's own are the child's to convert.
